value.overview: The Turquoise-browed Motmot (Eumomota superciliosa) is a colorful Central American bird recognized by its turquoise brow, black facial markings, green body, and long tail ending in racket-shaped tips. It is especially associated with dry forests, woodland edges, scrub, and other fairly open habitats. Unlike many forest birds, it often sits conspicuously on exposed branches, fences, or wires while watching for prey. In Costa Rica, it is a characteristic bird of the northwestern Pacific lowlands.
value.classification: The Turquoise-browed Motmot belongs to the motmot family, Momotidae, in the order Coraciiformes. It is the only species in the genus Eumomota.
value.identification: This medium-sized motmot has predominantly green plumage, a turquoise-blue crown and brow, a black eye stripe and throat patch, and warm cinnamon or rufous tones on the belly and breast. Its most distinctive feature is the long tail, whose central feathers have bare shafts ending in rounded, racket-like tips. The sexes are similar. It often perches upright and motionless, then makes short flights to capture prey or return to the same perch.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southeastern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, El Salvador, and Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a resident and is most characteristic of the northern Pacific region, especially Guanacaste, the Gulf of Nicoya area, and nearby dry lowlands and foothills. It favors tropical dry forest, open woodland, forest margins, scrub, plantations, pasture with trees, and secondary growth, generally avoiding dense, continuously humid rainforest. It occurs locally to roughly 800 meters in the Guanacaste foothills.
value.migrationStatus: Turquoise-browed Motmots are generally resident rather than long-distance migrants. In Costa Rica, the species is considered a year-round resident of the northwestern Pacific region, although local movements may occur as birds respond to food, rainfall, and nesting conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding pairs excavate long burrows in earthen banks, sandy river margins, road cuts, quarries, or other suitable soil. Nest tunnels may extend well over a meter and end in a nesting chamber. The species usually lays a small clutch of white eggs, commonly about three to six. Both adults participate in nest excavation, incubation, and care of the young. In Costa Rica, nesting activity is associated with the seasonal cycle of the Pacific dry-forest region, but timing can vary with local rainfall.
value.dietFeeding: The Turquoise-browed Motmot eats a broad range of animal prey, including beetles, grasshoppers, caterpillars, butterflies, spiders, worms, lizards, and other small vertebrates. It hunts from a low or exposed perch, dropping or flying down to seize prey on the ground, in vegetation, or occasionally in the air. Larger prey may be beaten against a branch before being swallowed or carried to nestlings. Small fruits may also be eaten.
value.behavior: This motmot is often seen sitting quietly for long periods, using a favorite perch to scan its surroundings. When disturbed, it may remain unusually still, allowing close approach. Its distinctive tail-wagging display is commonly associated with alertness or signaling to another bird. Individuals and pairs defend territories and may call repeatedly from conspicuous perches. The species is usually encountered singly, in pairs, or in small family groups, especially around nesting areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable, although detailed population estimates are limited and local abundance can vary with habitat conditions.
